To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) CNNs are able to outperform the state of the art in gender recognition on the LFW dataset; 2) CNNs are also able to outperform SVMs using local binary pattern (LBP) features in gender recognition on LFW; 3) adding contextual information improves gender recognition on GROUPS, and 4) CNNs trained on a large dataset of weakly labelled images can be used to generalise to new datasets.

(i) CNNs of different depths perform differently on the same task and the same dataset; (ii) the performance of the same CNNs is affected by the contextual information of the images; and (iii) CNNs trained on a large dataset of weakly labelled images are capable of generalising to new datasets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of gender classification systems, and the evaluation of their performance on a large number of weakly labelled training images, and on a large number real-world test images.
the following questions: How do deep convolutional neural networks perform in gender classification compared to other state-of-the-art approaches?
the following questions: (1) What is the best approach for classifying the gender of people in images?

1) the performance of the CNNs is better than that of the SVM approach; 2) the performance of CNNs with contextual information is better than that without; 3) the performance of cross-database classification is better than that on the same database; 4) the performance of deeper CNNs is better, although the difference in the performance is not significant.
the best approach for gender classification is to use a convolutional neural network trained on millions of weakly labelled images.

we have shown that: (1) deep learning can be used to achieve state of the art results in the gender classification problem, (2) large amounts of training examples are required to achieve this, and (3) the use of contextual information improves performance.

we have demonstrated that CNNs are the state-of-the-art approach for gender classification, that large amounts of data are necessary to train CNNs to generalise to new databases, and that the addition of contextual information improves classification accuracy.
the combination of deep learning with weakly supervised learning is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on gender recognition, even on cross-database classification.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, given enough training data and using a CNN architecture, it is possible to generalise to new datasets and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.

the combination of a deep neural network architecture with a large training set of images can achieve state-of-the-art results on the LFW dataset, and that the same architecture is also able to generalise to other datasets, even if the images were collected in different environments.
